q: What does Lightwave Logic do, in one sentence?
a: It designs electro-optic polymers, plastics whose molecules react to voltage, that let chips switch light on and off very fast with very little power, and it plans to sell and license them to companies building optical links for AI data centers.
On the Nasdaq under the ticker LWLG. It moved up from the OTCQB in 2021. Any regular brokerage account that offers US stocks can trade it.

q: Where is the company based and who runs it?
a: Englewood, Colorado, where it also has its chemistry labs and cleanroom. Yves LeMaitre has been CEO since December 2024.

q: What is a modulator, and why does it matter?
a: A modulator turns electrical data into pulses of light so it can travel over fiber. Every optical link in a data center needs them. Faster, lower-voltage modulators mean more data per link and less power.
Lightwave Logic's family of in-house-designed chromophores, the light-sensitive molecules inside its polymers. It's the company's core IP.

q: Weren't polymers supposed to be unreliable?
a: That was the classic objection. In July 2025 the latest Perkinamine polymer passed the Telcordia GR-468 85/85 damp-heat test (85°C, 85% humidity), and the company later reported more than 2,000 hours on the same test. Full device-level qualification is done with customers as they reach later stages.

Silicon (carrier-depletion) modulators, thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN), barium titanate (BTO), indium phosphide and electro-absorption lasers. Each trades off speed, voltage, power, cost and how easily it fits standard foundries.

By selling its polymer, licensing its technology (upfront and milestone fees), earning royalties when customer products ship in volume, and charging development fees before that. It doesn't plan to make chips or transceivers itself.

Very little, typically tens of thousands of dollars a quarter from its 2023 license and development fees. Meaningful revenue depends on customers reaching production, which management targets for 2027.

The five Stage 3 programs are with unnamed Fortune Global 500 companies under NDA. Named relationships include foundries (Tower Semiconductor, GlobalFoundries via GDSFactory, SilTerra via Luceda, AMF), and in October 2026 Hon Hai (Foxconn) showed a transceiver demo using LWLG polymers.

The company's design-win ladder: Stage 1 technology selection, Stage 2 product design, Stage 3 prototype to final product, Stage 4 production ramp. Five programs are in Stage 3 and none is in Stage 4 yet.

q: Why has it taken so long?
a: The core chemistry goes back to the 1990s. Getting a new material reliable, manufacturable in standard foundries and designed into customer products takes many years, and several past timelines slipped. The promise tracker shows what was hit and what was missed.

q: How much cash does it have, and how long will it last?
a: $95.9M in cash and marketable securities at June 30, 2026. Management says that funds operations through at least December 2027. Q3 figures arrive Nov 10.

q: Why does the share count keep rising?
a: Without meaningful revenue, the company funds itself by selling new shares (at-the-market sales and offerings). Shares outstanding rose from about 112M in 2022 to about 154M in 2026. That's dilution, and it's one of the main bear points.

q: Why is short interest so high?
a: About 28M shares were sold short as of mid-October 2026. Shorts are betting that timelines slip and dilution continues. If good news forces them to buy back shares, it can push the price up quickly, but that's not guaranteed.
There have been no open-market insider buys in the last two years. Insider transactions have been director sales, grants, option exercises and shares withheld for tax.

q: What would prove the bull case?
a: A Stage 4 production commitment, a signed supply/license agreement with the lead customer, and production revenue on the 2027 timeline.
Stage 3 programs stalling or dropping out, the 2027 production target slipping without explanation, a competing material winning the same sockets, or heavy dilution before revenue arrives.
